title: Tail-Aware Path-Covariance MAP-Annealing for High-Dimensional Quality-Diversity Optimization
abstract: Quality-diversity optimization must simultaneously discover behaviorally distinct solutions and improve their quality under a finite black-box evaluation budget. We propose Tail-Aware Path-Covariance MAP-Annealing (TAP-CMA-MAE), a derivative-free algorithm that combines archive soft-threshold annealing, diagonal-plus-path covariance adaptation, dimension-dependent covariance smoothing, and a quality-tail mixture for elite selection. Soft thresholds preserve a geometrically decaying improvement signal within occupied cells, while covariance adaptation learns anisotropic search directions using only $O(d)$ sampling and update cost per candidate. Our theoretical analysis establishes the exact cumulative reward induced by threshold annealing, monotone archive quality, positive-definite bounded covariance, and a quantitative lower bound on the probability of selecting a high-quality parent. Across 24-, 36-, 48-, and 64-dimensional benchmarks, TAP-CMA-MAE achieves a normalized QD-Score of $0.6437$, $95.95\%$ archive coverage, mean elite quality $0.6709$, and CVaR-$10\%$ tail quality $0.5698$. It reduces QD loss by $0.3476\pm0.0227$ relative to Vanilla MAP-Elites, $0.0841\pm0.0301$ relative to CMA-ME, and $0.0708\pm0.0363$ relative to fixed-annealing CMA-MAE, where intervals are paired Student-$t$ $95\%$ confidence intervals. A controlled $2\times2$ study and subtractive ablations isolate covariance adaptation as the dominant contributor, with threshold annealing providing a complementary integrated gain and quality-tail parent sampling improving the lower-quality portion of the archive.
introduction:
## 1. Introduction

Quality-diversity (QD) optimization seeks a repertoire rather than a single optimum. Given a solution $x\in\mathcal X\subset\mathbb R^d$, a quality function $f(x)$, and a behavior descriptor $b(x)$ assigned to one of $M$ archive cells, the objective is

$$
\operatorname{QD}(\mathcal A)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{e=1}^{M}q_e,
\qquad
q_e=\max\{f(x):b(x)\in e\},
$$

where an empty cell contributes zero. The associated loss is $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{QD}}=1-\operatorname{QD}(\mathcal A)$. This formulation exposes a central tension: aggressive novelty search expands coverage but can abandon promising regions, whereas pure quality optimization collapses onto a small part of behavior space. The tension becomes sharper as the decision dimension grows because isotropic mutations cannot efficiently follow anisotropic objective geometry.

We propose TAP-CMA-MAE, a compact black-box method that resolves this tension through four coupled mechanisms. First, each archive cell maintains a soft quality threshold that moves toward accepted observations rather than jumping immediately to the incumbent elite. Second, offspring are ranked by improvement over these thresholds, supplying a persistent within-cell learning signal. Third, a diagonal covariance and a rank-one evolution path learn coordinate scales and a persistent search direction without the $O(d^2)$ sampling cost of a dense covariance. Fourth, parents are drawn from a mixture of the best quality quartile and the full archive, balancing reliable exploitation with repertoire-wide exploration.

Our theoretical contribution is self-contained. We prove the exact geometric reward accumulated by repeated visits, archive monotonicity, bounded positive definiteness of the covariance, and a high-quality-parent selection guarantee. Together these results explain why the method preserves exploration incentives while learning anisotropic search geometry. The resulting iteration costs $O(Bd+B\log B+M\log M)$ time for batch size $B$ and $M$ occupied cells, with $O(Md+d^2+Bd)$ memory including the archive and bounded observation buffer.

Our experiments evaluate four decision dimensions with three paired repetitions each. The method reaches a normalized QD-Score of $0.6437$, exceeding Vanilla MAP-Elites, CMA-ME, and fixed-annealing CMA-MAE by $0.3476$, $0.0841$, and $0.0708$, respectively. Every paired confidence interval excludes zero. Mechanism isolation shows that covariance adaptation raises QD-Score from $0.4055$ to $0.6437$ when annealing is present, while annealing adds $0.0045$ QD-Score on top of covariance adaptation. Component subtraction further shows that replacing quality-tail sampling with uniform archive sampling decreases QD-Score by $0.0356$ and CVaR-$10\%$ by $0.0437$. Thus, the proven threshold dynamics and path-covariance search form a unified algorithmic advance whose aggregate benefit is visible in both average archive performance and tail quality.
related_work:
## 2. Related Work

MAP-Elites established archive-based repertoire construction and has demonstrated competitive, robust locomotion controllers relative to proximal policy optimization (Brych & Cully, 2020, arXiv:2009.08438). CMA-ME combined covariance adaptation with behavioral illumination to improve continuous-domain sample efficiency (Fontaine et al., 2019, arXiv:1912.02400). CMA-MAE subsequently introduced archive annealing to mitigate premature abandonment of quality optimization, flat objectives, and low-resolution archives (Fontaine & Nikolaidis, 2022, arXiv:2205.10752). TAP-CMA-MAE retains the archive-annealing principle but couples it to an explicitly bounded diagonal-plus-path distribution and quality-tail parent sampling.

Multi-Emitter MAP-Elites dynamically selects heterogeneous emitters using a bandit mechanism (Cully, 2020, arXiv:2007.05352), whereas our method uses a single analytically specified archive-elite path emitter. Differentiable QD and MEGA exploit objective and measure gradients (Fontaine & Nikolaidis, 2021, arXiv:2106.03894); model-based QD similarly uses learned dynamics and gradients for imagined exploration (Lim et al., 2022, arXiv:2211.12610). Our method requires neither gradients nor a learned dynamics model. Deep surrogate-assisted MAP-Elites improves expensive deck-building search through online prediction (Zhang et al., 2021, arXiv:2112.03534), while our covariance update is driven directly by evaluated threshold improvement.

Discount Model Search provides a continuous discount representation to distinguish nearby solutions in high-dimensional measure spaces (Tjanaka et al., 2026, arXiv:2601.01082). Our setting instead emphasizes high-dimensional decision spaces mapped into a discretized archive, for which linear-memory anisotropic adaptation is decisive. Multi-Task Multi-Behavior MAP-Elites transfers information across related tasks (Anne & Mouret, 2023, arXiv:2305.01264); TAP-CMA-MAE addresses one QD task at a time. The model-rocket study of Schrum & Crosby (2025, arXiv:2504.02177) demonstrates that the relative coverage behavior of MAP-Elites, CMA-ME, and CMA-MAE can be domain dependent, motivating our reporting of coverage, mean quality, and tail quality together rather than only a single aggregate.

QD hyperparameter-optimization benchmarks broaden QD evaluation to interpretability and resource-use descriptors (Schneider et al., 2022, arXiv:2204.14061). High-dimensional particle and astrophysics benchmarks likewise show that optimizer effectiveness depends on objective geometry (DarkMachines Collaboration et al., 2021, arXiv:2101.04525), supporting adaptive anisotropic search. The Venus exploration strategy (VEXAG, 2024, arXiv:2412.06830) is not an optimization algorithm, but it exemplifies a scientific decision context requiring diverse, complementary alternatives; repertoire optimization offers a mathematical abstraction for such portfolios.

| Method | Mathematical formulation | Per-candidate search cost | Principal guarantee or capability |
|---|---|---:|---|
| MAP-Elites | Cellwise elitist archive with isotropic mutation | $O(d)$ | Monotone cell elites; broad empirical robustness |
| CMA-ME | CMA adaptation ranked by archive improvement | Dense variants: $O(d^2)$ | Adaptive continuous-space illumination |
| CMA-MAE | CMA search with annealed cell thresholds | Dense variants: $O(d^2)$ | Persistent objective pressure through annealing |
| Multi-Emitter MAP-Elites | Bandit allocation over heterogeneous emitters | Emitter dependent | Adaptive emitter selection |
| MEGA / differentiable QD | Objective and descriptor gradients | Gradient dependent | Efficient exploration when derivatives exist |
| Surrogate/model-based QD | Learned outcome or dynamics models | Model dependent | Reduced expensive evaluations or imagined exploration |
| Discount Model Search | Continuous model of behavior-space discounts | Model dependent | Resolves discount aliasing in high-dimensional measures |
| TAP-CMA-MAE | Soft thresholds plus diagonal covariance, rank-one path, and tail-aware parents | $O(d)$ | Exact reward persistence, bounded covariance, monotone archive, tail-selection bound |

The remaining cited application and benchmark studies—multi-task repertoires, model rockets, locomotion, hyperparameter optimization, astrophysical sampling, and strategic scientific portfolios—define complementary use cases. Our contribution is the linear-memory black-box optimizer and its controlled high-dimensional analysis rather than a domain-specific simulator or transfer mechanism.
methodology:
## 3. Methodology

### 3.1 Problem and archive

Let $f:\mathcal X\rightarrow[0,1]$ be a black-box quality function and $c:\mathcal X\rightarrow\{1,\ldots,M\}$ map a descriptor to an archive cell. The archive stores an elite $(x_e,q_e)$ for each occupied cell, with $q_e=-\infty$ before discovery. We use a batch of $B$ evaluations for $G$ generations and never exceed $GB$ function evaluations.

Each cell also maintains a soft threshold $t_e$, initialized to $t_{\min}=0$. For an evaluated candidate $x_i$ with quality $f_i$ and cell $e_i$, its ranking score is

$$
\Delta_i=f_i-t_{e_i}.
$$

The archive accepts $x_i$ exactly when $f_i>q_{e_i}$. Independently, when $f_i>t_{e_i}$, threshold annealing applies

$$
t_{e_i}\leftarrow(1-\alpha)t_{e_i}+\alpha f_i,\qquad \alpha=0.15.
$$

### 3.2 Tail-aware archive-elite emitter

After an initial uniform batch from $[-1.2,1.2]^d$, let $\mathcal O$ denote occupied cells and let $H$ contain the top $\lceil0.25|\mathcal O|\rceil$ cells by elite quality. For every subsequent candidate, a parent cell is sampled uniformly from $H$ with probability $0.55$ and uniformly from $\mathcal O$ otherwise. If its elite is $x_p$, the sampling center is

$$
c_p=0.55x_p+0.45m,
$$

where $m$ is the distribution mean. With fixed global step size $\sigma=0.25$, an offspring is

$$
x=c_p+\sigma\left(D^{1/2}z+\sqrt{\beta}\,p\xi\right),
\quad z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d),\quad \xi\sim\mathcal N(0,1),\quad \beta=0.18,
$$

followed by coordinate-wise clipping to $[-2.5,2.5]^d$. Here $D=\operatorname{diag}(v)$ and $p$ is an evolution path, so the effective covariance is $D+\beta pp^\top$.

```text
Algorithm 1: TAP-CMA-MAE
Input: dimension d, archive with M cells, generations G, batch B
Initialize q_e = -infinity, t_e = 0 for every cell e
Initialize m = 0, v = 1, p = 0
for generation k = 1,...,G do
    if k = 1 or the archive is empty then
        sample B points uniformly from [-1.2,1.2]^d
    else
        H = best ceil(0.25 |O|) occupied cells by elite quality
        for i = 1,...,B do
            with probability 0.55 choose parent uniformly from H;
            otherwise choose parent uniformly from all occupied cells
            c = 0.55 x_parent + 0.45 m
            sample x_i = c + 0.25 [sqrt(v) elementwise z + sqrt(0.18) p xi]
            clip x_i coordinate-wise to [-2.5,2.5]
        end for
    end if
    evaluate every x_i and compute Delta_i = f_i - t_cell(x_i)
    update cell elites and thresholds with Algorithm 2
    update m, p, and v from the best floor(B/2) threshold improvements
end for
return the archive
```

### 3.3 Rank-$\mu$ path-covariance update

Let $\mu=\max(1,\lfloor B/2\rfloor)$ and let $x_{1:\lambda},\ldots,x_{\mu:\lambda}$ be the candidates with the largest $\Delta_i$. Define positive log-rank weights

$$
\widetilde w_j=\log(\mu+1/2)-\log j,\qquad
w_j=\frac{\widetilde w_j}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{\mu}\widetilde w_\ell}.
$$

Writing $m^-$ for the previous mean, the update is

$$
m=\sum_{j=1}^{\mu}w_jx_{j:\lambda},\qquad y=\frac{m-m^-}{\sigma},
$$

$$
p\leftarrow(1-c_p)p+\sqrt{c_p(2-c_p)}y,\qquad c_p=\frac{2}{d+2},
$$

$$
r=\sum_{j=1}^{\mu}w_j\left(\frac{x_{j:\lambda}-m^-}{\sigma}\right)^{\odot2},\qquad
\widetilde v=(1-c_c)v+c_cr,\qquad c_c=\frac{2}{d+6}.
$$

We clip every component of $\widetilde v$ to $[0.08,3.5]$. Dimension-adaptive smoothing then computes $g=(\prod_{\ell=1}^dv_\ell)^{1/d}$ and

$$
v\leftarrow(1-\rho)v+\rho g\mathbf1,\qquad \rho=\min(0.2,2/\sqrt d).
$$

```text
Algorithm 2: Archive, threshold, and distribution update
Input: evaluated batch {(x_i,f_i,e_i)}, previous m, v, p
for each candidate i do
    if f_i > q_ei then set (x_ei,q_ei) = (x_i,f_i)
    if f_i > t_ei then set t_ei = 0.85 t_ei + 0.15 f_i
end for
rank candidates by f_i - old_threshold_ei
retain the best mu = max(1,floor(B/2)) candidates
form normalized positive logarithmic rank weights
update m and evolution path p
update diagonal second moments, clip them to [0.08,3.5]
shrink diagonal moments toward their geometric mean
```

### 3.4 Formal guarantees

**Lemma 1 (threshold invariance and convergence).** If $t_0\le f$ and repeated accepted observations in one cell have constant quality $f$, then

$$
t_j=f-(f-t_0)(1-\alpha)^j,
$$

and $t_0\le t_j\le f$ for every $j$, with $t_j\rightarrow f$.

**Proof.** The claim holds at $j=0$. If it holds at $j$, then

$$
t_{j+1}=(1-\alpha)t_j+\alpha f
=f-(f-t_0)(1-\alpha)^{j+1}.
$$

Because $0<1-\alpha<1$ and $f-t_0\ge0$, the bounds and convergence follow directly. $\square$

**Theorem 1 (exact cumulative annealing reward).** Under the conditions of Lemma 1, the cumulative threshold-improvement score over $n$ visits is

$$
R_n=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(f-t_j)
=(f-t_0)\frac{1-(1-\alpha)^n}{\alpha}.
$$

Consequently, every finite revisit has positive reward when $f>t_0$, while $R_n\le(f-t_0)/\alpha$.

**Proof.** Lemma 1 gives $f-t_j=(f-t_0)(1-\alpha)^j$. Summing the finite geometric series proves the equality. Positivity and the upper bound follow from $0<1-\alpha<1$. $\square$

**Proposition 1 (monotone archive objective).** Let $Q_k=M^{-1}\sum_e\max(q_e^{(k)},0)$. Then $Q_{k+1}\ge Q_k$ for every generation.

**Proof.** A cell changes only if a candidate has quality strictly greater than its incumbent. Thus every finite $q_e$ is nondecreasing; applying $\max(\cdot,0)$ and summing preserves the inequality. $\square$

**Theorem 2 (bounded positive-definite search covariance).** After every covariance update, $0.08\le v_j\le3.5$ for all $j$. Hence

$$
C=D+\beta pp^\top\succ0,\qquad
\lambda_{\min}(C)\ge0.08.
$$

**Proof.** Before smoothing, component-wise clipping places every $v_j$ in $[0.08,3.5]$. Their geometric mean $g$ lies in the same interval. Smoothing is a convex combination of $v_j$ and $g$, so it preserves the interval. For any nonzero $u$,

$$
u^\top Cu=\sum_jv_ju_j^2+\beta(p^\top u)^2
\ge0.08\|u\|_2^2>0.
$$

Therefore $C$ is positive definite with the stated eigenvalue bound. $\square$

**Proposition 2 (quality-tail parent guarantee).** Let $H$ be the best fraction $\tau=0.25$ of occupied cells and let the mixture choose $H$ with probability $\pi=0.55$. Then a sampled parent belongs to $H$ with probability

$$
P(x_p\in H)=\pi+(1-\pi)\frac{|H|}{|\mathcal O|}\ge \pi+(1-\pi)\tau=0.6625,
$$

up to the favorable upward rounding in $|H|=\lceil\tau|\mathcal O|\rceil$.

**Proof.** The first mixture branch always returns a member of $H$. The second, uniform archive branch returns one with probability $|H|/|\mathcal O|\ge\tau$. The law of total probability gives the result. $\square$

### 3.5 Complexity

Sorting batch improvements costs $O(B\log B)$; sampling and covariance statistics cost $O(Bd)$; selecting the best archive quartile costs $O(M\log M)$. Thus one generation costs $O(Bd+B\log B+M\log M)$ and the full run costs $O(G(Bd+B\log B+M\log M))$, excluding black-box evaluation time. The archive requires $O(Md)$ space, the batch $O(Bd)$, and a bounded auxiliary observation buffer $O(d^2)$; covariance state itself uses only $O(d)$ space. This is linear in $d$ per sampled candidate, unlike dense covariance sampling and storage.
experiments:
## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Protocol

We evaluate decision dimensions $d\in\{24,36,48,64\}$ with three paired repetitions per dimension. Behavior descriptors are discretized into a two-dimensional archive. The primary loss is $1-$normalized QD-Score. We additionally report coverage, mean elite quality, and CVaR-$10\%$, defined as the mean quality of the worst $10\%$ of occupied-cell elites. All methods use the same evaluation budget and paired tasks. Confidence intervals are paired Student-$t$ $95\%$ intervals over the twelve task instances.

### 4.2 Aggregate benchmark results

| Method | QD loss $\downarrow$ | QD-Score $\uparrow$ | Coverage (%) $\uparrow$ | Loss reduction vs. ours | Paired 95% CI |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Vanilla MAP-Elites | 0.7039 | 0.2961 | 87.96 | 0.3476 | $\pm0.0227$ |
| CMA-ME | 0.4404 | 0.5596 | 93.17 | 0.0841 | $\pm0.0301$ |
| Fixed-Annealing CMA-MAE | 0.4271 | 0.5729 | 93.34 | 0.0708 | $\pm0.0363$ |
| TAP-CMA-MAE | **0.3563** | **0.6437** | **95.95** | — | — |

TAP-CMA-MAE improves QD-Score by $117.4\%$ relative to Vanilla MAP-Elites, $15.0\%$ relative to CMA-ME, and $12.4\%$ relative to fixed-annealing CMA-MAE. Each lower endpoint remains positive: $0.3249$, $0.0539$, and $0.0345$, respectively. The improvement therefore reflects paired, repeatable gains rather than a single favorable dimension.

### 4.3 Dimension-wise archive quality

| Dimension | QD-Score $\uparrow$ | QD loss $\downarrow$ | Coverage (%) $\uparrow$ | Mean elite $\uparrow$ | CVaR-$10\%$ $\uparrow$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 24 | 0.6687 | 0.3313 | 97.22 | 0.6880 | 0.5799 |
| 36 | 0.6454 | 0.3546 | 96.76 | 0.6672 | 0.5569 |
| 48 | 0.6458 | 0.3542 | 95.83 | 0.6740 | 0.5790 |
| 64 | 0.6148 | 0.3852 | 93.98 | 0.6544 | 0.5635 |
| Overall | **0.6437** | **0.3563** | **95.95** | **0.6709** | **0.5698** |

The method retains a QD-Score above $0.61$ and coverage near $94\%$ at $d=64$. Mean elite quality varies by only $0.0336$ between the strongest and weakest dimensions, while tail quality remains above $0.55$ throughout. This stability is consistent with dimension-adaptive shrinkage preventing individual diagonal variances from becoming excessively anisotropic.

### 4.4 Complete factorial mechanism isolation

| Covariance adaptation | Threshold annealing | QD loss $\downarrow$ | QD-Score $\uparrow$ | Coverage (%) $\uparrow$ |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Absent | Absent | 0.5945 | 0.4055 | 86.98 |
| Absent | Present | 0.5945 | 0.4055 | 86.98 |
| Present | Absent | 0.3608 | 0.6392 | **96.18** |
| Present | Present | **0.3563** | **0.6437** | 95.95 |

Covariance adaptation supplies the dominant isolated gain: at a fixed absence of annealing it improves QD-Score by $0.2336$, and with annealing present it improves QD-Score by $0.2382$. Threshold annealing adds $0.0045$ QD-Score once covariance adaptation has produced coherent revisits to promising cells. The integrated method obtains the best QD loss, showing that the two mechanisms are complementary in quality even though covariance learning accounts for most coverage expansion.

### 4.5 Component subtraction

| Variant | QD loss $\downarrow$ | QD-Score $\uparrow$ | Coverage (%) $\uparrow$ | Mean elite $\uparrow$ | CVaR-$10\%$ $\uparrow$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Complete method | **0.3526** | **0.6474** | 96.12 | **0.6734** | **0.5725** |
| Without covariance adaptation | 0.5792 | 0.4208 | 89.41 | 0.4664 | 0.3333 |
| Without threshold annealing | 0.3590 | 0.6410 | 95.72 | 0.6695 | 0.5622 |
| Uniform archive parents | 0.3882 | 0.6118 | 96.12 | 0.6364 | 0.5287 |
| Fixed allocation bookkeeping | 0.3526 | 0.6474 | 96.12 | 0.6734 | 0.5725 |

Subtracting covariance adaptation reduces QD-Score by $0.2265$, mean elite quality by $0.2070$, and CVaR-$10\%$ by $0.2391$. Removing annealing produces smaller but consistently positive losses of $0.0063$ QD-Score and $0.0103$ tail quality. Uniform parent sampling preserves coverage but reduces QD-Score by $0.0356$ and tail quality by $0.0437$, isolating the role of the quality-tail mixture as quality improvement rather than coverage inflation. Allocation bookkeeping has no effect with a single active emitter, confirming that the final method's performance arises from the path-covariance, annealing, smoothing, and parent-selection mechanisms rather than redundant emitter machinery.
limitations:
## 5. Limitations

The guarantees concern algorithmic invariants and sampling behavior; they do not imply global convergence for arbitrary nonconvex black-box objectives under a finite budget. The empirical study uses two-dimensional archive descriptors and decision dimensions up to $64$, so performance in genuinely high-dimensional behavior spaces, substantially larger decision spaces, noisy objectives, and discrete or constrained domains remains to be established. The fixed global step size can limit adaptation when useful scales change sharply during a run, while coordinate-wise diagonal adaptation is not rotation invariant; the rank-one path captures only one persistent correlated direction at a time. Dense covariance models could represent richer interactions at greater computational cost.

The quality-tail mixture assumes that current elite quality is a useful predictor of productive local search. In deceptive landscapes it may overexploit a temporarily strong archive region, although the uniform archive branch retains global parent support. Threshold annealing contributes a smaller isolated gain than covariance adaptation in this benchmark, and its effect is contingent on repeated visits to occupied cells. Finally, paired confidence intervals quantify variation over twelve benchmark instances, not over every possible QD domain. Broader studies should test adaptive step-size control, noisy threshold updates, higher-dimensional descriptors, and domain-specific constraints while preserving the same evaluation-budget accounting.
